summary: Updates TLS-based EAP types such as EAP-FAST, EAP-TTLS, and TEAP, and possibly PEAP, to work with TLS 1.3, following what RFC 9190 did for EAP-TLS.

eli5.summary: Wi-Fi login methods built on secure web connections get updated to use the newest version of them.

questions: how does teap work with tls 1.3
can tls 1.3 session tickets bypass eap authentication
subtitle: How EAP methods built on TLS, such as TEAP, EAP-FAST, EAP-TTLS and PEAP, move to TLS 1.3.

tldr.problem: EAP-TLS was updated for TLS 1.3 in RFC 9190, but other EAP types that run inside TLS use key derivation functions that no longer apply to TLS 1.3, so they are incompatible with it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9427 defines new key derivation functions based on the TLS-Exporter, adds the logical EAP Type to the derivation, and spells out the other changes TLS 1.3 forces: application data handling, session tickets, client certificates, identities and resumption.
tldr.outcome: TEAP, EAP-FAST, EAP-TTLS and, where applicable, PEAP and vendor-specific methods can run over TLS 1.3. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4851, RFC 5281 and RFC 7170, and it is itself updated by RFC 9930.

today: RFC 9427 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2023. It updates RFC 4851, RFC 5281 and RFC 7170, and it is itself updated by RFC 9930.

sections.title: Why TLS-Based EAP Methods Needed an Update
sections.content:
EAP (the Extensible Authentication Protocol) lets a network and a client run many different login methods. EAP-TLS was updated for TLS 1.3 in RFC 9190. Many other EAP types also depend on TLS: EAP-FAST (RFC 4851), EAP-TTLS (RFC 5281) and TEAP (RFC 7170). The RFC says it is possible that many vendor-specific methods, such as PEAP, depend on TLS as well.

All of these methods use key derivation functions that are no longer applicable to TLS 1.3, so they are incompatible with it. RFC 9427 fixes this by defining new key derivation functions. It also discusses the implementation differences between TLS 1.3 and earlier versions.

In general, everything in RFC 9190 applies to the other methods. They MUST follow it unless this document says otherwise. The main differences are that RFC 9190 uses the EAP-TLS Type (value 0x0D) in its calculations, while other methods use their own Type, and that the protected success indication is needed only during resumption for the other methods.
sections.eli5: The tunnel that protects your login got a new version, and the old way of making secret keys does not fit it. This document says how to make the keys the new way.

sections.title: Key Derivation with the TLS-Exporter
sections.content:
Key derivation depends on the logical Type of the EAP method. For Types below 254 it is the one-octet Type. For Expanded Types it is 0xFE || Vendor-Id || Vendor-Type. For example, the Type for PEAP is simply 0x19.

The shared definitions come from RFC 9190 and use the TLS-Exporter: Key_Material is 128 octets and Method-Id is 64 octets, both exported with the logical Type as context. The MSK is the first 64 octets of the key material and the EMSK is the next 64. The exporter labels of EAP-TLS are reused, and only the dependency on the Type is added, which makes the derivation method specific.

One warning applies: unlike TLS 1.2 and earlier, the TLS-Exporter output depends on the length passed in. Implementations MUST pass the correct length rather than a large length followed by truncation, because the truncated result is different.

These definitions apply in full to EAP-TTLS and PEAP. Vendor-defined and other TLS-based methods are RECOMMENDED to use them too, since there is no compelling reason to differ.
sections.eli5: Both sides stir the same secret together with the name of the login method and get matching keys. If you ask for a key of the wrong length, you get a different key altogether, so you must ask for exactly the right size.

sections.title: Method-Specific Changes
sections.content:
TEAP and EAP-FAST. The Protected Access Credential (PAC) is functionally equivalent to a TLS 1.3 session ticket, so PAC use and PAC provisioning are deprecated and no longer part of these methods with TLS 1.3. The inner-method session key, the compound keys and the outer MSK and EMSK are all derived with the TLS-Exporter using labels such as EXPORTER: teap session key seed, and the TEAP Compound MAC uses the HMAC algorithm negotiated for HKDF in the TLS 1.3 key schedule. EAP-FAST uses the same derivations with its own Type, and its T-PRF is replaced by the TLS-Exporter.

EAP-TTLS. The implicit challenge for the CHAP, MS-CHAP and MS-CHAPv2 inner methods is derived with the label ttls challenge and no context value. Its length is 17 octets for CHAP and MS-CHAPv2 and 9 octets for MS-CHAP.

PEAP. With crypto binding, the PRF+ function stays as it is, but the Tunnel Key is taken from the Key_Material defined in this document. The older method MUST NOT be used.

Client certificates. They are still allowed with TEAP, EAP-FAST, EAP-TTLS and PEAP. But if the certificate is accepted, the peer MUST go on to further authentication in the inner tunnel, and if there is none the server MUST reject the session. Using a client certificate with no inner method is forbidden, and EAP-TLS should be used for that instead. TEAP also needs an Identity-Type TLV when a client certificate is sent outside the tunnel.
sections.eli5: Each login method has its own little quirks. Old shortcuts such as pre-made passes are retired. And a certificate alone is not enough for these methods, because they must also check the person inside the tunnel.

sections.title: Application Data and Session Tickets
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 can keep negotiating after the handshake is complete, a state it calls CONNECTED. Earlier versions never sent application data along with the Finished message, so some implementations took a Finished message to mean that the tunnel was ready for a fresh round trip. That assumption is wrong for TLS 1.3. Implementations MUST check for application data once the TLS session is established, before another round of TLS negotiation.

TLS 1.3 also allows NewSessionTicket messages after the server has received the client Finished message. Implementations MUST NOT send or expect application data while negotiation is still in progress, and they MUST discard without examining any application data from a negotiation that fails.

Many TLS libraries send a ticket right after Finished by default. A malicious peer could then obtain a ticket, close the session and resume with it, skipping the inner authentication. So the server MUST NOT let any ticket resume a session unless inner authentication succeeded. Implementations SHOULD NOT send NewSessionTicket messages until inner authentication has completed, and servers MUST invalidate or discard tickets of sessions that end in EAP Failure. The ticket SHOULD be sent along with other application data when possible.
sections.eli5: A ticket is like a wristband that lets you back in without checking again. If you hand it out before the guard checks who you are, someone could grab the wristband and walk straight in, so wristbands are only given after the check.

sections.title: Inner and Outer Identities
sections.content:
Tunneled methods carry two identities. The outer identity is sent in the clear and used to route the request. The inner identity travels inside the TLS tunnel with the credentials, for example an EAP Response/Identity for PEAP or the User-Name attribute for EAP-TTLS.

The outer identity SHOULD use an anonymous Network Access Identifier (NAI) realm, which gives privacy and still lets the session be routed in a AAA framework. The inner identity MUST NOT use an anonymous NAI realm, and servers MUST fail authentication if a peer uses an anonymous inner identity. Anonymous network access should use EAP-TLS without peer authentication instead. Inner identities SHOULD NOT contain an NAI realm.

The RFC warns against mixing organizations, for example a routing realm of one organization with an inner identity from another. At worst the other domain could harvest credentials. A server that receives an inner identity for a realm it is not authoritative for MUST reject it. Using a hosted AAA provider's realm or a cloud identity provider's identity this way is NOT RECOMMENDED, because changing providers would then require updating every device. Dynamic discovery as in RFC 7585 makes it cheaper to change one domain's configuration. The RFC concedes that existing deployments with differing realms cannot be forbidden.
sections.eli5: The name on the outside of the envelope only tells the mail carrier where to deliver it, so it can be vague. The name on the letter inside must be real, and the receiver should only open letters for people they actually know.

sections.title: Session Resumption
sections.content:
Resumption works as in RFC 9190, and it is the same for every TLS-based EAP Type except for the value of the Type field. If a session is resumed, the server MUST send the protected success indication, one octet of 0x00, inside the TLS tunnel. The peer MUST check for that octet and fail authentication if it is missing. If either side starts an inner method, that method MUST be followed and inner authentication MUST NOT be skipped.

All EAP servers and peers MUST support resumption for all TLS-based EAP methods, though they can choose not to resume a particular session, for example for policy reasons. Enabling and using resumption is RECOMMENDED, because it cuts round trips, latency and load on the server and on systems such as credential databases.

Resumption across different EAP Types is forbidden. Servers MUST NOT resume a session across Types and MUST reject a resumption whose Type differs from the original authentication, for instance authenticating with EAP-TLS (Type 13) and resuming with EAP-TTLS (Type 21).
sections.eli5: If you have already shown your ID today, you can show your wristband instead of the ID. But a wristband from the swimming pool does not work at the cinema: it must be used for the same kind of login it came from.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Section 5 of RFC 9190 is included by reference. The RFC calls updating these methods to TLS 1.3 highly important, because newer security protocols can significantly improve the security and privacy of a network. For PEAP, some derivations still use HMAC-SHA1. They are left unchanged for interoperability and minimal changes, since there are no known security issues with HMAC-SHA1 and the derived data is exchanged inside the tunnel.

The central risk is a time-of-check, time-of-use problem. A server may send a NewSessionTicket before the user has been authenticated. A malicious client could abort the session and use the ticket to resume without ever being authenticated. So servers MUST NOT assume a user is authenticated just because a session is resuming. They SHOULD track whether inner authentication completed and tie that status to each ticket, and if they cannot tell, they MUST run the inner authentication in the resumed tunnel before granting access.

Protected success and failure indications exist for RFC 9190 in both full authentication and resumption, but other methods provide them only for resumption. Some inner methods, such as PAP, CHAP and MS-CHAP in EAP-TTLS, cannot signal the result inside the tunnel. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to deprecate such inner methods when tickets cannot be used, and SHOULD use EAP-GTC instead of PAP, EAP-MD5 instead of CHAP, and MS-CHAPv2 or EAP-MSCHAPv2 instead of MS-CHAPv1. New TLS-based methods MUST provide protected indications inside the tunnel.
sections.eli5: The danger is a person sneaking in with a pass that was given out too early. So the guard either hands out passes only after checking you, or checks again whenever the pass is used.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA added five labels to the TLS Exporter Label registry defined by RFC 5705. They are used only for TEAP, and each is marked as not OK for DTLS and as recommended. The labels are EXPORTER: teap session key seed, EXPORTER: Inner Methods Compound Keys, EXPORTER: Session Key Generating Function, EXPORTER: Extended Session Key Generating Function and TEAPbindkey@ietf.org.
sections.eli5: The new secret-key names were written in an official public list so nobody reuses them by mistake.

viz.caption: KEY DERIVATION FOR TLS-BASED EAP TYPES WITH TLS 1.3 (RFC 9427)

data.title: Shared derivation
data.code:
Key_Material = TLS-Exporter("EXPORTER_EAP_TLS_Key_Material",
                            Type, 128)
Method-Id    = TLS-Exporter("EXPORTER_EAP_TLS_Method-Id",
                            Type, 64)
Session-Id   = Type || Method-Id
MSK          = Key_Material(0, 63)
EMSK         = Key_Material(64, 127)

cells: Own session key seed and compound key labels
Same as TEAP with the EAP-FAST Type
PAC no longer used; T-PRF replaced
Shared definitions; challenge from ttls challenge label
No protected result with PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP
